choices.english: may be seen to proceed in due order
choices.why: κόσμος here is 'order'; the old English 'As the world unfolds in the necessary world' misread it.

choices.term: ἐκ καρποῦ τῆς ὀσφύος αὐτοῦ τὸ κατὰ σάρκα
choices.english: one would be born of the fruit of his loins according to the flesh (Acts 2:30)
choices.why: The quoted words are the Acts 2:30 form of the promise; the subject is left implied as in the Greek.
Old English 'stripped of the former glory, saying he has been stripped of it' lost the one-person/whole-race point.

pass_a_gloss: (so that the rendering of the thoughts) may appear proceeding in fitting order, come, and before the others let us touch the interpretation (theoria) in the psalm mentioned before. The divine David knew as a prophet that according to the unlying and divine promise 'from the fruit of his loins (the one) according to flesh' would come to be, except that he was not ignorant that being God by nature he would let himself down into our condition at the right time. He converses therefore in the eighth psalm and makes his words to him as to man and at once God, recognizing as one God the one from both. For this reason he says 'Lord, our Lord, how wonderful your name in all the earth, because your magnificence was lifted above the heavens'; for where at all or among whom was Christ not marveled at? Or how was his magnificence and the conspicuousness of glory not lifted even above the heavens? If indeed it is true that 'in the name of Jesus Christ every knee bends of heavenly and earthly and underground (beings) and every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord to the glory of God the Father.' For that the divine singer says such things to the Word having appeared in human form and united to flesh, (388) the things following would easily show; for he said 'from the mouth of infants and sucklings you prepared praise.' For when he raised Lazarus from the dead, he was marveled at by all, 'and having found a young donkey he sat on it', when also children, having taken 'the palm branches of the date palms', honoring him with the fitting acclamations, said 'Hosanna to the son of David, blessed the one coming in the name of the Lord.' And the others rebuking them, Christ said 'Did you not read that from the mouth of infants and sucklings you prepared praise?' Seeing then the Son having become man and all but riding on the colt, he was fittingly astounded, pondering that, that he is seen having let himself down to so much littleness although being God by nature; then the blessed David, seeing no other occasion of the having been emptied except us alone, whom it was necessary both to take out of corruption and sin and to snatch from tyrannical hands, I mean those of the devil, deems the mystery of the economy with flesh worthy of all wonder. For this reason he says 'Lord, what is man that you remember him, or son of man that you visit him?' For what is the nature of man as toward God? And why do I say this? What is the human race? And as what portion would those on earth be reckoned, as toward, I say, the orders of the holy angels? But even if man is nothing at all by nature and number, the Creator did not overlook us, for he remembered us also and deemed us worthy of visitation, as having perished; he who also at the beginnings of bringing us into existence, made us less a little beside the angels, but crowned us with honor and glory, and set us over the works of his hands, and subjected all things under our feet. And of the whole song the aim is in these things, but the divine Paul philosophizes greatly and skillfully turns around our condition, which had fallen sick, into newness through Christ; for new creation are the things in him, and the old things passed by, and all things have become new; this the Holy Spirit says also through one of the prophets: 'Take courage Zion, let your hands not be slackened; the Lord your God in you mightily to save you and he will renew you in his love.' Paul then shows us naked of the glory given of old; on account of this he says 'But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him.' And surely we do not think, having chosen to think right things, that he says such things about one man, but as in one person signifying the man in general, he says him to have been robbed of the participation of the renown given of old. And what the construction of the whole argument is, and what the conclusion of the skill, it is necessary to tell. For he shows (continues).
pass_b_english: may be seen to proceed in due order, come, before anything else let us take up the interpretation of the psalm we have mentioned. The inspired David knew as a prophet that, according to the unlying and divine promise, one would be born "of the fruit of his loins according to the flesh" (Acts 2:30); yet he was well aware that, being God by nature, he would let himself down into our condition in due time. So in the eighth psalm he converses with him and addresses his words to him as to man and at the same time God, recognizing as one God the one who is from both. That is why he says, "O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth! For your majesty is lifted up above the heavens" (Psalm 8:1). For where at all, or among whom, was Christ not wondered at? Or how was his majesty, and the splendor of his glory, not lifted up even above the heavens, if indeed it is true that "at the name of Jesus Christ every knee bows, of things in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father" (Philippians 2:10-11)?

That the inspired singer says such things to the Word, who appeared in human form and was united to flesh, what follows would easily show. For he said, "Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise" (Psalm 8:2). When he had raised Lazarus from the dead, he was wondered at by all, and "finding a young donkey, he sat on it" (John 12:14); and then the children took "the branches of the palm trees" (John 12:13) and honored him with the acclamations due to him, saying, "Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!" (Matthew 21:9). When others rebuked them, Christ said, "Have you never read, 'Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise'?" (Matthew 21:16). So, seeing the Son made man and all but riding on the colt, David was rightly astounded, as he pondered this: that one who is God by nature is seen to have let himself down to so great a lowliness. Then, seeing no other reason for the self-emptying than us alone, whom it was necessary to rescue from corruption and sin and to snatch from the tyrant's hands (I mean the devil's), the blessed David holds the mystery of the economy in the flesh worthy of all wonder. That is why he says, "Lord, what is man, that you remember him, or the son of man, that you visit him?" (Psalm 8:4). For what is the nature of man compared with God? And why do I say this? What is the human race? And at what share would those on earth be reckoned, compared, I mean, with the ranks of the holy angels? But even if man is nothing at all, in nature and in number, the Creator did not overlook us. He remembered us too and thought us worthy of his visitation, as men who had perished; he who at the beginning, when he brought us into being, made us a little lower than the angels, but crowned us with honor and glory, set us over the works of his hands, and put all things in subjection under our feet (Psalm 8:5-6).

Such is the aim of the whole song. But the inspired Paul reasons very deeply, and with great skill he turns our sick condition around into newness through Christ. For what is in him is a new creation: the old things have passed away, and all things have become new (2 Corinthians 5:17). The Holy Spirit says this through one of the prophets too: "Take heart, Zion, let your hands not grow slack. The Lord your God is in you, mighty to save you, and he will renew you in his love" (Zephaniah 3:16-17). So Paul shows that we are stripped of the glory given us long ago; that is why he says, "But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him" (Hebrews 2:8). Since we have chosen to think rightly, we surely do not think that he says such things about one man. Rather, signifying man in general as in one person, he says that he has been robbed of his share in the renown given long ago. παροισθέντων ψαλμῷ θεωρίας ἁψώμεθα. ᾔδει ὡς προφήτης ὁ θεσπέσιος ∆αυεὶδ ὅτι
κατὰ τὴν ἀψευδῆ τε καὶ θείαν ὑπόσχεσιν "ἐκ καρποῦ τῆς ὀσφύος αὐτοῦ τὸ κατὰ σάρκα"
γενήσεται, πλὴν οὐκ ἠγνόηκεν ὅτι Θεὸς κατὰ φύσιν ὑπάρχων ἐν τοῖς καθ' ἡμᾶς ἑαυτὸν
καθήσει κατὰ καιρόν. διαλέγεται τοίνυν ἐν τῷ ὀγδόῳ ψαλμῷ καὶ τοὺς πρὸς αὐτὸν
ποιεῖται λόγους ὡς πρὸς ἄνθρωπον ἅμα καὶ Θεὸν ἕνα τὸν ἐξ ἀμφοῖν ἐπιγινώσκων Θεόν.
ταύτῃτοί φησι "Κύριε ὁ Κύριος ἡμῶν, ὡς "θαυμαστὸν τὸ ὄνομά σου ἐν πάσῃ τῇ γῇ, ὅτι
ἐπήρθη ἡ "μεγαλοπρέπειά σου ὑπεράνω τῶν οὐρανῶν·" ποῦ γὰρ ὅλως ἢ παρὰ τίσι
Χριστὸς οὐ τεθαύμαστο; ἢ πῶς οὐκ ἐπήρθη καὶ ὑπεράνω τῶν οὐρανῶν ἡ μεγαλοπρέπεια
αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸ τῆς δόξης περιφανές; εἴπερ ἐστὶν ἀληθὲς ὅτι "ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι "̓Ιησοῦ

δόξῃ καὶ καταστήσας μὲν ἐπὶ τὰ ἔργα τῶν χειρῶν αὐτοῦ, πάντα δὲ ὑποτάξας ὑπὸ πόδας
ἡμῶν.
Καὶ τῆς μὲν ὅλης ᾠδῆς ὁ σκόπος ἐν τούτοις, φιλοσοφεῖ 38 δὲ λίαν ὁ θεσπέσιος
Παῦλος καὶ περιίστησιν εὐτέχνως νενοσηκότα τὰ καθ' ἡμᾶς εἰς καινότητα διὰ Χριστοῦ·
καινὴ γὰρ κτίσις τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ καὶ τὰ μὲν ἀρχαῖα παρῆλθε, γέγονε δὲ πάντα καινά· τοῦτό
φησι καὶ δι' ἑνὸς τῶν προφητῶν τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ Ἅγιον "Θάρσει Σιὼν, μὴ παρείσθωσαν αἱ

καὶ οὐ δήπου φρονοῦμεν, ὀρθὰ φρονεῖν ᾑρημένοι περὶ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου τὰ τοιάδε λέγειν
